COMMISSION SUPPORTS SEMINAR FOR PORT STATE CONTROL SURVEYORS. The Commission of the European Communities has reached an agreement with the Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control Secretariat to help finance organization of the 5th "Seminar for Surveyors" which is to be held in Lisbon, Portugal, on 24, 25 and 26 June. These seminars for surveyors, being regular features of the Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control, have until now been financed partly by the host country and partly by the other 13 countries which participate in the Memorandum of Understanding. The system of Port State Control provides for regular inspection of ships calling in at the ports of all signatory countries. Support for the Lisbon seminar reflects the Commission's view that this inspection system is a key weapon in making ships safer, ensuring satisfactory crewing conditions and reducing maritime pollution. The financial participation of the EC in this particular seminar should be seen in the framework of the "European Year of the Environment". The Lisbon seminar, organized by the maritime authorities of Portugal, will deal mainly with the consequences of the coming into force in April this year of the important Annex II to the MARPOL 73/78 Convention. This Annex is designed to prevent pollution of the marine environment from ships that carry noxious liquid substances in bulk. In order to control the processing and the disposal of chemical residues, the Convention strongly emphasizes the involvement of port states - hence the need for surveyors with the right expertise.

COMMISSION STATEMENT IN RESPONSE TO NEWS OF A DELIVERY OF RADIOACTIVE EUROPEAN MILK TO GHANA. The Commission was surprised to hear the news from Ghana concerning a Community delivery of highly radioactive skimmed milk powder. The Commission is anxious to emphasize that deliveries of food aid products are accompanied by certificates issued by approved European laboratories to the effect that the products comply with Community standards (370 becquerels/kg for skimmed milk). The delivery in question was certified as having a level of radioactivity well below this ceiling. The Commission would also point out that, on the basis of these certificates, the specialist firm designated by the Ghanaian authorities themselves issued an attestation of conformity at the time of loading. Furthermore, a second check on samples taken by the same specialist firm at the time of the products' arrival in Ghana fully confirmed the low radioactive reading. Therefore, and in view of the information from Ghana, the Commission would like to have light thrown on this affair as soon as possible. It is sending without delay a representative of a specialist firm to Accra to carry out appropriate checks on the spot with the cooperation of the Ghanaian authorities, and also to take fresh samples so that further analyses can be made. The Commission has already told the Ghanaian authorities that it is willing that the laboratory to be designated to carry out these further checks be chosen by agreement.

IMPLEMENTATION OF ENVIRONMENT DIRECTIVES : COMMISSION DECIDES REASONED OPINIONS AGAINST MEMBER STATES. The Commission today adopted a series of reasoned opinions against several member states for their failure to implement properly a number of Community environment directives: 1. Greece: bathing beaches. With the exception of the area around Athens, the Greek government has not applied the Community directive on bathing water. Under this legislation, a member state should designate the main bathing beaches and apply Community quality standards. The Commission has decided on a reasoned opinion requiring full application of the directive. 2. Italy: pesticides in drinking water. Community legislation on drinking water lays down maximum levels for the presence of certain pesticides such as atrazine. In Italian national legislation levels have been specified which are 10 times higher than allowed under the directive. The Commission has decided to send a reasoned opinion to the Italian Government demanding changes in the legislation. 3. Nine member states: disposal of bottles. Member states should draw up programmes under the Community's bottles directive for reducing the tonnage and/or volume of bottles and other drinks containers going into household rubbish bins. The aim of the programme is to encourage recycling or reuse of drinks containers. Only three member states have so far fulfilled this requirement (Denmark, Ireland and the Netherlands) and the Commission has therefore decided to send the other member states a reasoned opinion requiring them to draw up the necessary plans. 4. France: imports of protected species. The Commission adopted a reasoned opinion against France last month for not respecting an agreement under the Washington Convention (CITES: international trade in species of flora and fauna threatened with extinction). The French authorities granted an import permit authorising the importation of 6 000 skins from Bolivia of the species Felis wiedii and Felis geoffroyi, so breaching a Community agreement not to accept the validity of Bolivian export licences, many of which are believed to be forged.

STRENGTHENING OF CONTROL MEASURES FOR FISHING ACTIVITIES. The Commission has approved a proposal for a Council regulation strengthening arrangements for surveillance of fishing. The Community regulations on this subject were originally adopted in June 1982, and have since been amended on a number of occasions to strengthen the requirements*, but experience shows that additions are needed. The new proposal concerns verification problems which arise where fishing vessels make landings outside the jurisdiction of the flag state. The additional arrangements concern mainly the following points: (a) the flag state may request the Member State of landing to provide rapid and detailed information on landings by the flag state's vessels; the Commission will be informed of such requests and will receive a copy of the information supplied. (b) the flag state may subject fishing by its vessels of a given stock to the possession of a licence. Where a Member State informs the Commission and the other Member States of the quota concerned, and circulates details of the licensed vessels, an offence is created under Community law of fishing or landing from the quota concerned unless the vessel concerned is licensed. (c) in the case of vessels which have committed an offence against conservation law, the flag state may, as an additional control measure, require them to show their catches on stocks subject to quota to the flag state's authorities before landing such catches in another Member State. A further Community offence is created of landing catches from such stocks in another Member State from such a vessel if the necessary certificate of inspection is not on board. (d) Member States of landing are required to apply a sufficient sanction when they discover these offences and also the offence of landing fish from a quota which is exhausted and of which the Commission has halted fishing. In the absence of such enforcement action, the Commission may decide that the landing in question shall be counted against the quota of the Member State of landing, or, if it has no relevant quota remaining, that the latter Member State shall compensate the flag state by making an appropriate transfer of fish to it. * Council Regulation (EEC) No 2241/87, of 23 July 1987, provides a consolidation of all the amendments to the original Regulation.

THE COMMISSION TAKES SPAIN TO THE COURT OF JUSTICE ON CHEMICAL WASTE. The Commission has decided to bring an action before the Court of Justice against Spain concerning pollution of the River Gallego with discharges containing hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH), originating from the manufacturing process of an insecticide called "Lindane", by a chemical firm at Sabinanigo (Huesca). The River Gallego supplies drinking water to a number of villages with a total population of around 4000. The Commission believes that this situation endangers both the health of the area's inhabitants and the environment. The Commission has taken this decision because the Spanish authorities have not acted to stop these discharges, which infringe Community legislation. Following a complaint, the Commission was able to determine that these discharges of waste containing HCH constitute an infringement of the Directives on toxic and dangerous waste, groundwater, surface water and drinking water. COMMISSION REFERS TO THE COURT OF JUSTICE ON TELEGRAM COSTS FOR IMPORTERS OF LIVING ANIMALS IN ITALY. the Commission decided to bring before the Court of Justice an action against Italy regarding the charging of telegram costs to importers of live animals. The matter of the costs of the telegrams which Italian veterinaries at border posts send to the Italian Ministry of Health, the Nucleo Antisofisticazioni1) of the Carabinieri and the mayors of the communes of destination pursuant to national provisions on veterinary checks in respect of imports of live animals from the other Member States, had earlier been referred to the Commission. The telegrams in question are mainly those which the authorities responsible for the checks upon importation sent to the competent local authorities when a consignment of animals, accompanied by a single health certificate, is split up and sent to several destinations in Italy. The telegrams notify the said authorities of the splitting up of the health documents presented at the border post and of any other relevant information concerning the veterinary checks. The Commission feels that making traders pay for telegrams which are required under current Italian legislation is tantamount to applying a charge which has an effect equivalent to customs duty and is, therefore, incompatible with the Treaty of Rome. For additional information, contact: G Guarneri 2363362 E Kaiser 2352210 1) Fraud Squad.

CONTAINERS OF LIQUIDS FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION : COMMISSION TAKES ACTION AGAINST SEVERAL MEMBER STATES. The Commission has decided to bring proceedings under Article 169 of the EEC Treaty against Belgium, France, Luxembourg and Portugal to ensure that Directive 85/339/EEC on containers of liquids for human consumption is properly applied. Article 3 of that Directive lays down that Member States shall draw up programmes for reducing the tonnage and/or volume of containers of liquids for human consumption. These programmes had to be implemented from 1 January 1987. The Commission has still not received programmes for Luxembourg, Belgium and Portugal. In the opinion of the Commission, the programme drawn up by France does not meet the requirements of the Directive. By contrast, as the Federal Republic of Germany adopted a programme for containers of liquids for human consumption in March 1989, the Commission has decided to end the infringement proceedings brought against that country.

COMMISSION BRINGS SPAIN BEFORE THE COURT OF JUSTICE FOR ITS FAILURE TO REGISTER FISHERY CATCHES. The Commission has decided to refer to the Court of Justice of the European Communities an infringement by Spain, which is not recording catches of species subject to TAC or to quotas in ICES divisions VI, VII and VIII and fished outside the 200-mile limit. The Spanish authorities consider that the TACs fixed by the Council apply only to that part of the ICES divisions in question which form part of the Community fishing zone. In fact, save in the case of explicit exceptions, the TACs cover all parts of the divisions mentioned. The Community's jurisdiction extends to the fishing activities of Member States' vessels in international waters. As a result of Spain's position, catches are not fully declared and species for which it has no quota are caught and landed. In addition, fishermen tend to declare they have fished in that part of the zone which is outside the 200-mile limit. Referral to the Court is the third and last stage in an infringement procedure, the first two stages of which involve a letter of notice and a reasoned opinion.

COMMISSION ASKS GERMANY TO ADOPT ITS LEGISLATION ON DRINKING WATER TO COMMUNITY LAW. The Commission makes the proper implementation of existing environmental legislation by Member States one of its primary objectives. Mr Ripa di Meana, Member of the Commission with responsibility for the environment, announced this policy at the beginning of his term of office stressing that it was also necessary to look into new forms of dialogue with national and regional authorities to encourage the implementation of Community provisions. The Commission has decided to send Germany a reasoned opinion because German legislation on drinking water only partially conforms to Community law. This reasoned opinion concerns Directive 80/778, adopted in 1980, which set quality standards for drinking water. Member States were obliged to bring their national legislation into line with the Directive by 1982 and to clean up their drinking water, if necessary, by 1985. The Federal Republic of Germany only carried out the necessary harmonization in 1986. Furthermore, it unilaterally gave itself more time, up to October 1989, to implement Parameter 55 which aims to limit pesticides in drinking water. The Commission is also of the opinion that several other German provisions do not conform to Directive 80/778. The Commission is particularly concerned by the fact that Article 4 of the German Trinkwasserverordnung allows the derogation of Community provisions, without the limits in Directive 80/778 being observed. According to information appearing in the German media the German government intended to use this Article to avoid fully implementing Directive 80/778 in Germany. The Commission recalls that in the Spring of 1989 it decided to open infringement procedures against Germany over the practical application of several Community directives on water. The procedures concern nitrate levels in surface and drinking water as well as pollution of ground and drinking water by pesticides. According to the Commission's information a large number of German citizens regularly receive drinking water with nitrate levels above the maximum concentrations authorized under the Community Directive (50 mg/litre). As regards pesticides, in some regions of Germany river water is filtered through the ground to recharge groundwater. However, it appears that certain pesticides are not eliminated by this method of filtration and add to groundwater pollution, in contravention of Community Directive 80/68. Also, in some regions, drinking water supplied to the consumer contains more than the maximum permitted concentrations of pesticides. The Federal Republic of Germany has not replied to, or commented on, the points put forward by the Commission. For further information contact: Mr C Stathopoulos: Tel. 2352463/2359667 Mrs E Kaiser: Tel. 2352210.

COMMISSION OPENS INFRINGEMENT PROCEDURE AGAINST GREECE FOR FAILURE TO COMPLY THE PROVISIONS GOVERNING IMPORTS OF CUTS OF BEEF. In December 1986 Greece was held liable by the Court of Justice of banning imports of certain cuts of fresh beef. A new law was adopted in August 1987, but did not terminate the breach which was the subject of the proceedings, since it maintained obstacles to the importation of fresh beef. Certain forms of cuts, imports of which were formerly banned, can now be imported and marketed. Some cuts of fresh beef can still not be imported into Greece, however. These are fresh meats cut, boned and put up in plastic bags and ready to be sold in butcher shops. The Commission decided recently, therefore, to initiate a new infringement procedure against Greece.

SHIPMENT OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE. The Commission has just adopted a proposal for a Directive which will make shipments of radioactive waste entering, leaving and moving within the Community subject to a system of authorization, notification and control. The aim of the proposal is to tighten up the administrative supervision of the movement of radioactive waste which was shown to be inadequate in relation to the events investigated by the European Parliament Committee of Inquiry on the handling and transport of nuclear material. The proposal was drawn up at the initiative of Mr RIPA DI MEANA, who stressed that the provisions of the proposal prevented any possible recurrence of worrying incidents like the Transnuklear/Mol affair in the future. Operations involving radioactive and nuclear wastes had to be carried out under the strictest possible controls and under the close supervision of the authorities. Activities which involve a risk resulting from ionizing radiation are covered in the Community by the provisions of the Council Directive of 15 July 1980. The proposal for a Directive that has been adopted adds the shipment of radioactive waste to the activities for which prior authorization from the competent authorities is required under that Directive. The proposal also gives details of the procedure for implementing the system. The system set out in the proposal is modelled on the system laid down in the Council Directive of 6 December 1984 on the supervision and control within the European Community of the transfrontier shipment of hazardous waste. It also contains a number of features taken from the Basle Convention of 22 March 1989 on the control of transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal, which was signed by the Commission on behalf of the Community on the day of its adoption. The proposed system is based essentially on the following measures: - every intended shipment of radioactive waste must be notified to the competent authorities of the Member State of destination of the radioactive waste. If the radioactive wastes are to be exported to a third State, their shipment must be notified to the competent authorities of the Member State of dispatch. In this case the notification must clearly indicate the agreement of the third State of destination;(1) - shipment may not be effected before the competent authorities have acknowledged receipt of the notification authorizing the shipment. - the competent authorities shall authorize shipment only when sufficient evidence has been submitted of the ability of the consignee to manage the radioactive waste properly. In the case of a shipment to a destination in a third State, the prior written consent of that State is required. - a general notification procedure may be used instead of the specific notification in the case of shipments of radioactive waste having the same characteristics and shipped under the same conditions. The general notification procedure may be applied, inter alia, to shipments of radioactive waste arising from medical practices. - a uniform consignment note must be used for all steps laid down by the system. ALPINE TRANSIT. Mr Karel Van Miert, European Commissioner for transport, held a meeting yesterday afternoon in Frankfurt with the German and Italian Transport Ministers, Mr Zimmermann and Mr Bernini, and the Austrian Transport Minister, Mr Streicher. The meeting, to take stock of the situation concerning the implementation of Austrian measures restricting night-time movements of lorries, had been proposed by Mr Van Miert after the German and Italian ministers had voiced concern over certain aspects of the implementation of the Austrian measures. At yesterday's meeting it was decided to set up a working group, with a Commission chairman, to examine the allegations of discrimination and other problems connected with transit. Agreement was also reached on the need for the three countries concerned to arrive at a trilateral agreement on rail transport and the development of combined transport for alpine transit. Mr Van Miert also stated that the Commission would expedite work to define the clean lorry, i.e. one which complies with tight pollution and noise standards. Mr Van Miert and the ministers agreed to meet again in the near future, after groups of experts have prepared the ground.

SWINE FEVER. On the recommendation of the EC's Veterinary Committee the Commission today (Thursday, September 6) decided to lift the various restrictions which had prevented Belgium from exporting meat to other Member States on account of a recent outbreak of swine fever disease. For "the Buffer-zone" comprising about one third of the country where 80% of pig production is concentrated, all restrictions are lifted, thus restoring free movement of trade. From September 10th, Belgium will be authorized to dispatch by sealed transport pigs slaughtered after September 7th as well as pig meat products emanating from the previously closed-off zones A, B, C and D Three other conditions govern the resumption of meat trade from these zones. The meat must: 1. have been submitted to a health examination at the herd of origin by a veterinarian designated by the competent veterinary authorities and found to have presented no sign of disease; this examination must have taken place within 24 hours of slaughter. originating from a herd where a random blood tast has been carried out and the result of the test is negative. which have been transported directly in a sealed means of transport from the herd of origin to the designated abattoir, the means of transport utilized must be cleaned and disinfected before and after each journey. The restrictions however, will continue to be applied to the Communes of Wingene and Pittem, to all parts of the Communes of Ardoole with the exception of the area west of the A 17 motorway, and to all parts of the Communes of Meulebeke, Tielt and Ruiselede with the exception of the area south-east of trunk road N 399 and trunk road N 37. The situation there will be reviewed by the Committee at its next meeting before the end of September.

THE COMMISSION PROTESTS TO THE AUSTRIAN GOVERNMENT AND REQUESTS SUSPENSION OF THE RESTRICTION ON ROAD HAULAGE. On 12 November Mr Van Miert, Member of the Commission, sent Mr Streicher, the Austrian Minister of Transport, a letter pointing out that the latest restrictions imposed by the Austrian government on traffic on the Inntal- Brenner motorway were not compatible with the agreement reached on 27 August between the Commission and the Member States most directly involved in transit traffic through Austria. At the same time Mr Van Miert urgently convened a meeting of the parties concerned, to be held before the end of the week. The restrictions affect the carriage of certain types of goods in heavy vehicles transiting Austria on the way from some of the German Laender to certain Italian regions.

PROTECTING CHILDREN AGAINST DANGEROUS TOYS. On 28 February, acting under the early warning system, the Belgian authorities sent the Commission detailed information pointing out the dangers to children from handling a toy grenade. The responsible authorities throughout the Community were warned of the dangers within two days of the notification from the Belgian authorities. They were rapidly able to look for the product in question on their market and, where necessary, take steps to withdraw this product which has injured several children, causing burns and the loss of fingers. In recent months the Member States have used the early warning system on several occasions (see Annex for recent notifications) even before taking formal action against the article in question. Mr Van Miert, the Commissioner responsible, considers that it would be desirable for this to happen automatically in future, and even more quickly than at present, in order to provide even greater consumer protection. These toy grenades should be withdrawn from the market under the "toys" directive since they fail to meet the essential safety requirement that toys must not be explosive. However, the early warning system will only become fully effective at Community level once it is incorporated into a general directive on product safety. In that context, following notification and as the last resort in the event of divergent action by Member States, all the responsible authorities of the Member States, in conjunction with the Commission, could consider adopting measures at Community level in order to ensure harmonized consumer protection throughout the Community./.

COMMISSION DECIDES TO TERMINATE INFRINGEMENT PROCEEDINGS AGAINST SPAIN CONCERNING THE AWARD OF PUBLIC WORKS CONTRACTS BY THE CONSORCI DE LA VILA OLIMPICA. The Commission's attention was drawn to the failure to publish, in breach of Directive 71/305/EEC, tender notices in respect of three contracts for the construction of housing, commercial premises and parking spaces. Investigation of the case revealed the source of the infringement: Consorci, an entity governed by public law and set up by the Banyoles Municipal Council and the Catalan Land Institute, was not regarded as a contracting authority within the meaning of the Directive. Not only has Spain acknowledged the infringement, but Consorci has also amended its articles of association so as to make the award of public works contracts subject to the Spanish provisions transposing Directive 71/305/EEC into national law. Since, in its view, the measures taken are fitting, the Commission has decided to terminate the proceedings.

PRIOR AUTHORIZATION SYSTEM FOR IMPORTS OF MILK AND MILK PRODUCTS. This infringement procedure concerned the conditions imposed by the Danish authorities on imports of milk and milk products from other Member States. Denmark had introduced a system of prior authorization and other preliminary formalities for all imports of milk products. The Commission departments had numerous contacts with the Danish authorities in the course of the infringement procedure and Denmark agreed finally to amend the requirements by adopting a new regulation (Decree No 478 of 22 June 1990). In the case of heat-treated milk, prior authorization and the other formalities have been replaced by the health certificate provided for in Council Directive 85/397/CEE It is worth noting also that the import into Denmark of cheese and butter is no longer subject to the presentation of a health certificate. However, pending adoption of harmonized measures at Community level, Denmark will continue to require health certificates for a number of other milk products. In the present state of Community law, the Commission does not object to the use of these certificates for the limited range of products for which the Danish authorities still require them. In view of the above circumstances, the Commission has decided to terminate the infringement procedure.

THE EC SAFETY MARK FOR TOYS. the Council of the Ministers of the European Communities adopted a directive on safety for toys. All the Member States have now transposed this Community directive into national legislation. The Directive stipulates that all toys placed on the Community market must bear the EC mark. This can be placed on the toy itself or its packaging or, if the toys are small, on a label or note. Although this mark is mainly for the benefit of the national inspection authorities, the Commission would like consumers to know what it means. The mark provides evidence of the manufacturer's declaration that he has designed and manufactured the toy in accordance with the requirements of the Community directive on safety for toys of 3 May 1988 (see Press Release No 267 of 3 May 1988). For the consumer the EC mark on toys sold in the Community signifies that they must conform with high safety standards. A proposal for a general regulation to establish the precise conditions for affixing and using an EC mark for industrial products has now been put before the Council of Ministers of the Communities.

FISHERIES: THE COMMISSION TAKES MEASURES TO PROTECT DOLPHINS. Following an initiative by Mr Manuel Marín, Member of the Commission with responsibility for cooperation and development and fisheries, the Commission has adopted a proposal for a regulation banning the use of purse seine nets in fishing for tuna where dolphins may also be present. This method of tuna fishing, practised in the waters of the central and eastern Pacific, caused the death of some 130 000 dolphins in 1986 alone. - - - The non-selective use of purse seine nets in fishing operations carried out in tuna shoals where dolphins are present can result in the pointless capture and death of these mammals. International public opinion and a large number of organizations involved in nature conservation have expressed their opposition to this type of fishing where it results in the death of marine mammals. The Commission today decided to propose a regulation amending Regulation (EEC) No 3094/86 laying down certain technical measures for the conservation of fishery resources. Under the proposal, any use of purse seine nets which might cause the death of marine mammals (especially in the waters of the central and eastern Pacific) will be prohibited. Through this measure the Commission aims to ensure (as it already did in 1991 by banning fishing with large drift nets) that fishing methods are responsibly applied and do not cause the unnecessary death of non-commercial species. The proposal follows the guidelines in the Morris report on purse seine nets, adopted by the Parliament on 22 November 1991. Background The problem of dolphin deaths caused by fishing for tuna with purse seine nets is confined mainly to the waters of the IATTC (Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission: central and eastern Pacific). It is only in this region that a biological association is found between dolphins and yellowfin tuna. In the waters of the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean, for example, the phenomenon does not occur: fishing with purse seine nets does not therefore cause the death of marine mammals. According to the most reliable estimates, some 133 000 dolphins were killed in 1986 as a result of tuna fishing in the Pacific, as against an average of 45 000 per year between 1979 and 1985. Since then, international pressure has brought about a significant reduction in killings. The Community fleet which fishes with purse seine nets (some 80 vessels) does not fish at the moment in the area where the dolphin/tuna association occurs, but fishes rather in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. The Commission proposal mainly aims to prevent Community vessels from moving to the waters of the central and eastern Pacific - where they are not currently present - and using there the purse seine net fishing method.

THE COMMISSION DECIDES TO CLOSE AN INFRINGEMENT PROCEDURE AGAINST DENMARK. Infringement 92/5131 Denmark Public Procurement Closure of the file Københavns Lufthavne A/S (Copenhagen Airports) launched a restricted procedure for the purchase of snow clearing equipment in September 1993 and published a notice in the O. J. E. C No S 185/37 of 23 September 1992 to that effect. The Commission received a complaint against this procedure in which it was alleged that "EC rules on open tendering" would have been infringed. However, before the Commission had the possibility of reacting otherwise than through an acknowledgment of receipt, it was informed by the plaintiff that the Danish authorities had annulled the original procedure and launched a new restricted procedure. A notice to that effect has been published in the O. J. E. C No 233/40 of 1 December 1992. The Commission has therefore decided to close this file.

COMMISSION ADOPTED A MODIFICATION ADAPTING THE DIRECTIVEON DANGEROUS SUBSTANCES TO TECHNICAL PROGRESS. Council Directive 67/548/EEC(1) as last amended by Council Directive 92/32/EEC(2) contains in its Annex I a list of dangerous substances for which uniform classification and labelling have been decided at Community level. The Directive proposed by Commissioner Paleokrassas which has just been adopted by the Commission is the 19th Adaptation to Technical Progress of Directive 67/548/EEC This Directive modifies Annex I in order to bring it into line with the changes introduced by Council Directive 92/32/EEC (the 7th Amendment). In addition, the classification and labelling of a number of substances or groups of substances already in Annex I have been revised and brought up to date on the basis of new scientific information. A further 70 new entries have been added to Annex I This adaption introduces into Annex I 19 substances or groups of substances classified as carcinogens. The Commission as part of its Action Programme against cancer has given a very high priority to this work. This Directive is one of the main Community measures in the area of chemicals control and is of considerable importance to chemical industry in particular. The large number of changes and amendments to this Directive makes it difficult to ensure a comprehensive view of this Directive. In order to remedy this, the Commission will shortly be presenting a Consolidated version of this Directive to the Council, so that the whole text of this Directive will be available in a single coherent document. (1) OJ N° 196 of 16/08/1967, p. 1 (2) OJ N° L 154 du 05/06/1992, p.1.

POLICING OF FISHERIES IN THE NETHERLANDS. To remedy the shortcomings revealed some years ago in the inspection of fisheries, more specifically in the regulation of sole catches, the Netherlands set up a new policing system in 1993. It is based to a certain extent on the acceptance of shared responsibility by the fishermen's organizations. On 15 February a major inspection operation (involving Netherlands and Belgian authorities) was conducted in and around the quayside auction market at Vlissingen. Commission staff had already been informed of preliminary findings by the Netherlands fisheries authorities in mid-January. During 1993 inspections were carried out by DG XIV officials in the Netherlands and it was agreed with the Netherlands authorities that the Commission would conduct an evaluation of the effectiveness of the Netherlands policing system. The infringements discovered this week confirm the need for such an inquiry, which will be facilitated, in terms of thoroughness and effectiveness, by the application of certain provisions of the new Regulation on fisheries control, adopted in 1993 and brought into effect at the beginning of this year. In particular the new rules allow inspections without advance warning. The arrangements for the investigation will be adopted after consultation between Commission staff and the Netherlands authorities in 1994. In answer to an invitation sent out by DG XIV in January, officials from the fisheries inspection authorities of all the Member States are due to attend a meeting in Brussels on 22 and 23 February in order to try and speed up the implementation of the new control rules, which pave the way for inspections of all aspects - markets, structures and resources. In the view of Mr Paleokrassas, Commission Member responsible for fisheries, the success of the new Community rules depends on efficient policing and the efforts of the Member States, in liaison with the fishermen themselves and the Commission, to ensure that it is properly carried out.

PROTECTION OF WILD BIRDS. the Commission proposed an amendment to the 1979 Directive on the conservation of wild birds incorporating in a new annex the method developed by the Member States in the Committee for adaptation to scientific and technical progress. Criticism levied by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds in particular has prompted the Commission to make the following clarifications: - The Directive does not set limits for hunting but merely specifies that birds may not be hunted during their return to their nesting sites. - The date of 31 January does not figure in any Community text; on that date, many species have not begun their return migration. - The Court of Justice judgement of 191.1994 did not fix a date either, but reiterated the principles laid down in the Directive and stressed that methods for determining the dates of the close of the hunting season intended to, or having the effect of, excluding a given percentage of birds from the protection granted by the Directive are illegal. - The Court is referring here to the methods adopted by the French auhorities and does not call into question the method adopted by the management committee for the Directive (Ornis Committee), which is composed of representatives of the twelve Member States. - This method, which the Commission proposes to incorporate in an annex to the Directive, will not prolong the hunting season in France, which closes on 28 February at the latest pursuant to the French Rural Code. - This method, already published by the Commission in November 1993 in the report on application of the Directive (COM/93/572 of 23111993), is the fruit of the work of a group of scientists designated by Member States to assist the Ornis Committee.

ITALIAN FRAUD RING CRACKED. UCLAF, the Commission's Coordination of Fraud Prevention Unit, together with the Italian Guardia di Finanza, has just completed an investigation in Malta, one of the countries receiving consignments of meat from the Italian BLANGINO group which is suspected of fraud against the Community budget. A vast fraud ring has been cracked in Italy: to date nearly 200 people are under investigation and 50 of them have been arrested. The fraud is thought to involve some ECU 43 million (80 billion lire). The case is being handled by the public prosecutor in Turin. The fraud was a sophisticated form of smuggling involving a huge volume of merchandise: 25 000 head of live cattle and 4 500 tons of beef were imported from Eastern Europe ostensibly for processing and reexport, in which case no customs duties would be payable. In fact, the merchandise was secretly released onto the internal market for sale without paying customs duties. Low- quality meat and scraps from processing in Italy were then exported to Malta in place of the misappropriated meat. With the support of the Maltese customs authorities, a team from UCLAF spent 5 days investigating what the merchandise actually was and where it really ended up. The Maltese veterinary authorities also provided invaluable assistance. Building on its cooperation with the Italian authorities (the investigation is being led by the Guardia di Finanza), UCLAF staff will continue to play an active role in whatever investigations may be necessary to bring all the implications of this fraud to light. Together with the Italian authorities, UCLAF will ensure that the money is recovered and that those responsible are brought to justice.

CONCLUSIONS OF THE MEETING ON THE ALBACORE FISHERY ON FRIDAY 29 JULY 1994(COMMISSION, SPAIN, UNITED KINGDOM, IRELAND, FRANCE). It was confirmed by all parties, that no vessel may keep on board, or use for fishing, one or more drifnets whose individual or total length is more than 25 kilometres. In cases of apparent infringements, Member States shall take appropriate and effective measures without delay, within the context of their own national legislation, to ensure compliance with and the enforcement of Community regulations. In this context, Member States and the Commission examined certain measures adopted or envisaged by Member States, such as confiscation of illegal drifnets at sea, and the escorting of the alleged infringing vessels to port. On board inspections will be carried out only by patrol vessels of the flag Member State. EC inspectors will monitor and be present at these inspections as frequently as possible. During such inspections, and in the presence of national inspectors, the Commission Inspectors shall have access to the different compartments and all documentation relevant to fishing activities and shall ensure correct measurement of the length of driftnets. They will receive precise instructions and procedures in order to achieve the maximum efficiency of enforcement and cooperation between Member States. Observations of the apparent infringement of vessels of another flag will be communicated to the flag Member States authorities, who will transmit this information to any of its fishery protection vessels in this area. Detailed inspections will be carried out, subject to operational constraints. Any driftnet lost by a vessel should be reported to the national authorities which will communicate this information to the Commission. If possible, this information will also be transmitted to all fishery protection vessels in this area, and to other Member States authorities. Whenever an unattended drifnet is recovered by any fishery protection vessel of a Member State, this must be communicated to the Commission which will transmit the information to other Member States. If the owner of the drifnet can be identified, the return of the net will be carried out between the authorities of the Member States involved and under the auspices of the Commission. Member States will transmit to the Commission a detailed description of the measures used to undertake control in harbours. The Commission will analyze these measures and transmit its comments to the Member State and if appropriate suggest amendment. In addition to monitoring the Albacore fishery, the Member States and the Commission considered that the inspection scheme anticipated, could be used to carry out additional control and monitoring of catches and landings of other species in ICES sub-areas VII and VIII These matters will be considered further at a meeting in the near future. La Commission se réjouit de la volonté et de l'esprit de coopération manifestés par les Etats membres, matérialisés par la présence sur zone à l'heure actuelle de navires de contrôle britanniques, espagnols, français et irlandais, accueillant des inspecteurs communautaires. La Commission considère toutefois qu'une solution durable ne pourra être trouvée sans que des dispositions de contrôle supplémentaires ne soient adoptées par le Conseil

EMERGENCY HUMANITARIAN AID FOR VICTIMS OF THE ALGERIAN EARTHQUAKE. In response to an appeal from the Algerian government, the European Commission Humanitarian Office (ECHO) has approved an initial package of emergency aid worth ECU 400 000 for victims of the earthquake which occurred in the small hours last Thursday morning in Mascara (western Algeria). The quake was one of the worst to hit the country in the past decade. Provisional estimates put the toll at around a hundred dead or injured. Reports say damage is widespread and many people have been made homeless. Panic has also broken out in Oran, some 100 kilometres from Mascara, where tremors were also felt. ECHO has negotiated with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) for the aid to be channelled immediately to where it is needed.

COMMISSION PLANS TO TIGHTEN SAFETY ON RO-RO FERRIES. Commission proposes a Council regulation on the safety management of roll- on roll-off passenger ferries Under a new rule proposed by the EU Commission today, companies operating roll-on roll-of ferries would only be allowed to operate from EU ports if they sign up to a strict safety code. On the initiative of Neil Kinnock, the Commissioner responsible for Transport, the Commission will ask the European Council of Transport Ministers to adopt a Regulation obliging all companies operating a regular ferry service from ports in the European Union to implement the International Safety Management Code that has been drawn up by the International Maritime Organisation. At present, too many companies operating public ferry services do not have efficient safety codes. A regulation takes instant effect in all Member States, bypassing the need for lengthy procedures to write the measure into national law. The proposal is made in response to a request by the Council on 22 December last year that the Commission draw up the necessary legislation before 1 July 1996. Today's initiative would not only bring the Code into mandatory effect a full two years earlier, but would also ensure that safety management systems are effectively controlled by the Member States. Neil Kinnock said: "Tragedies such as that of the Estonia or of the Herald of Free Enterprise cannot be allowed to happen again. Everyone who travels on ferries has the right to expect them to be safe and efficient. This is the first of a series of proposals I shall be making this year to ensure that safety is made the highest priority of all transport policy." The shipping industry has never had a common set of detailed safety management procedures covering everything from shore-based management practices and communications to emergency procedures. The adoption of this Regulation would mark a major breakthrough in ensuring that safety considerations are made an integral part of all shipping business.

"ESTAI" FOUND TO COMPLY WITH NAFO RULES - CANADIAN ASSERTIONS NOT PROVEN. Fisheries/European Union-Canada On Friday, 24 March, Community inspectors conducted an inspection of the Community fishing vessel "Estai", which returned to the port of Vigo in Galicia (Spain) on Thursday evening. No irregularities were found. The results of this inspection show that Canada's accusations that the "Estai" had been engaged in irregular fishing activities before it was arrested in international waters off Newfoundland on 9 March are unfounded. "Since I am not answerable to voters either in Newfoundland or in Vigo, I can tell you the results of the Community's inspection of the "Estai" without fear of appearing to defend one side or the other," said Mrs Bonino, the Commissioner responsible for fisheries. According to the Community inspectors, who had been dispatched to Vigo on Thursday morning, the vessel's cargo consisted of 170 tonnes of fish, including 150 tonnes of Greenland halibut. The composition of the catch (3% fish of 30 cm, 15% of 36 cm and 82% of over 40 cm) and measurements made of the four nets on board confirmed that they were in conformity with NAFO rules (mesh-size of 130 mm), showing that no abnormal use had been made of the gear carried. No secret hold or false flooring was discovered on the "Estai". The inspectors did find that there were two logbooks. The first one was almost full up and the master of the vessel had started a second in order to avoid an apparent break in the record of fishing activities. According to the Canadian inspectors, the ship was carrying 82% juvenile fish. They also said that there was a concealed second logbook and a secret fish compartment. These details were used to justify the arrest of the vessel in terms of better conservation of the halibut stock. "The concern to improve the conservation of fishery resources was evidently not the motive for Canada's action, but rather a desire to extend the country's jurisdiction to the high seas," Mrs Bonino concludes. The master of the "Estai" gave further details of the arrest of his vessel. No warning by radio or other means had been given by the Canadian authorities before they opened fire on it. The master also said that he ordered the net to be cast off on seeing the Canadian authorities making armed threats. He did say that the behaviour of the officers who then boarded his vessel had been correct. The master also reported that the "Estai" had been inspected by the Canadians on 17 January. The report on this inspection had still not been relayed to the authorities in the flag country, although the current NAFO rules required that authorities making an inspection are to inform the flag state within a reasonable period.

THIRD PILLAR TO BE RESTRUCTURED. "The Commission and the new Spanish Presidency have now decided to start a restructuring of the rather cumbersome decision routes in the Third Pillar. During my travels to the EU Capitals I have repeatedly heard demands for a smoother decision procedure", says Commissioner Anita Gradin responsible for Justice and Home affairs. When the Maastricht Treaty was implemented, the already existing structures in the informal cooperation in Home and Justice affairs were kept as they were. The new structures were simply superimposed on those already in place. The result is that the operational structures extend over five negotiating levels - Council, Coreper, Article K.4 Committee, steering groups and (16) working parties. The only decision-making level especially mentioned in the Treaty is the K4 Committee. Normally only three operational levels are found in the Community context. Mrs Gradin has discussed the problem with the Spanish Presidency and they will now together develop more efficient structures for the Third Pillar Cooperation.

THE COMMISSION RULES OUT INFRINGEMENT PROCEDURES AGAINST THE UNITED KINGDOMFOR THE NEWBURY BYPASS AND M 77. n the light of a decision from the European Court of Justice in August 1995 (C 431/92), the Commission has decided to interprete the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (Dir. 85/337/EEC) as requiring this assessment only for projects where the procedure for consent was started after 3 July 1988, i.e. after the latest date for transposing the Directive into national law. That means that the EIA Directive does not apply for two road projects, the Newbury Bypass, England, and the M 77, Scotland. Although development consent was given for these projects after 3 July 1988, lengthy consent procedures started well before that date. Consequently decisions to proceed with the road projects and the actual routing have to be considered a purely national matter. * *.

PUBLIC PROCUREMENT: INFRINGEMENT PROCEEDINGS INITIATED AGAINST FRANCE INCONNECTION WITH THE WORLD CUP STADIUM. The European Commission has decided to initiate infringement proceedings under Article 169 of the EC Treaty against France in connection with the award of a contract for the construction and operation of a large football stadium at Saint-Denis in the suburbs of Paris. The stadium is planned for the 1998 World Cup. The Commission has contacted the French authorities several times on this matter, but has not so far received satisfactory replies to its requests for information. On the basis of the information at its disposal, the Commission takes the view that the procedure followed for awarding the contract could be in breach of Directive 93/37/EEC The Commission's main concerns focus on respect of the consultation rules drawn up by the contracting authority and the conditions of the final concession contract. Under Article 169 of the Treaty, should France fail to produce a satisfactory reply within two months of receiving the letter of formal notice the Commission could decide to move on to the next stage in the procedure and deliver a reasoned opinion.

EMERGENCY HUMANITARIAN AID FOR FLOOD VICTIMS IN PAKISTAN. The European Union has decided to make ECU 200 000 of humanitarian aid available through the European Community Humanitarian Office (ECHO) for the victims of the recent floods in Pakistan. Continuous rain has devastated most of Pakistan's provinces. Heavy rain is normal in this region during the monsoon season, but this year it came early, has been especially heavy and has been aggravated by snow melt in the mountains. The flooding has cost human lives and affected nearly two million people, several hundred of whom have been evacuated and put up in camps. In response to the disaster which has struck the poorest areas of Pakistan, ECHO has decided to support a programme to distribute emergency needs (tents, blankets, clothes, cooking utensils) in Punjab and Sindh, the provinces worst affected. The partner selected to manage the operation is the International Federation of the Red Cross, which will delegate implementation to the Pakistan Red Crescent Society.

PUBLIC PROCUREMENT: INFRINGEMENT PROCEDURES AGAINST FRANCE AND PORTUGAL. The European Commission has decided to pursue infringement procedures according to Article 169 of the EC Treaty against France and Portugal for violations of Community rules on public procurement. France has been referred to the Court of Justice concerning the construction of a school in Wingles (Nord/Pas de Calais region) and Portugal is to be sent a reasoned opinion concerning a system for processing contaminated solid hospital waste. France - construction of a school in Wingles In the absence of reply to the reasoned opinion notified on 8 September 1995 to the French authorities in connection with the construction of the 'lycée' in Wingles, the Commission has decided to refer France to the Court of Justice for violation of the provisions of the Directive on public works contracts (71/305/EEC as amended by Directive 89/440/EEC). The contract, entrusted in 1993 to a local company, was the subject of a complaint. The Commission considers that the French authorities failed to fulfil their obligations under the Directive by publishing a contract notice quoting purely French qualifications without mentioning the equivalence of qualifications from other Member States and by confusing the various criteria envisaged at the time of the procedure in order to award the contract to the locally-established tenderer. Moreover, the French authorities have refused to send the relevant information requested by the Commission. Portugal - unit for the treatment of contaminated hospital waste The Commission has agreed to send a reasoned opinion to the Portuguese authorities with respect to an award procedure concerning the design, construction and operation of a unit for the treatment of contaminated hospital waste in the Lisbon area. The Commission's main concern is that the contracting authority decided to change the site of the unit during the course of the procedure. Indeed, while the contract notice indicated that the unit would be constructed in Beirolas, the Commission has been told that the new site of the unit will be at São João da Talha. Such a move constitutes a substantial change of the initially published conditions and thus a breach of EC public procurement rules (notably public works Directive 93/37/EEC). The Portuguese Authorities received a letter of formal notice dated 110795 requesting a reply within two months, but no reply has arrived to date. In the absence of a satisfactory reply to the reasoned opinion within 40 days of receipt, the Commission may decide to refer Portugal to the Court of Justice.

"URGENT NEED FOR ACTION TO CURB RADIATION RISKS FROM THE CHERNOBYLSARCOPHAGUS" - STATEMENT BY COMMISSIONER BJERREGAARD AND COMMISSIONER VANDEN BROEK. On the background of reports on increased radiation levels inside the sarcophagus covering Reactor Four at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant (NPP), Commissioner BJERREGAARD and Commissioner van den BROEK today issued the following statement: "Even if the cause for the recurring incidents of significantly increased levels of radiation inside the old sarcophagus for the moment is not fully established, the incidents clearly demonstrate the need to bring the potential risks related to the sarcophagus under a satisfactory control as soon as possible. We therefore urge the Ukrainian authorities to provide detailed information regarding the nature of the incidents reported. This information can be taken into account in the framework of the feasibility study under way concerning appropriate measures to be taken to ensure security related to the sarcophagus. A commitment to provide all relevant information to complete the feasibility study has been taken by the Ukrainian authorities in the context of the Memorandum of Understanding, signed on 20 December 1995 between G7 and Ukraine. As soon as the conclusions of this feasibility study will be available, probably in November 1996, the Commission is determined to contribute to the establishment of a safe and definitive solution to the problems linked to the sarcophagus".

COMPLAINT ON ANIMAL WELFARE. The Commissioner for Agriculture and Rural Development, Mr Franz FISCHLER, has received a complaint from Eurogroup for Animal Welfare that the provisions of the Directive on the welfare of animals in transport are not being respected as far as imports of horses from Eastern Europe through the Italian border posts of Gorizia, Fernetti and Prosecco are concerned. The substance of the complaint is that overloaded trucks with sick, injured and dead horses arrived at these border posts and that veterinary treatment, feed, water and rest was either not provided or was totally inadequate. Reacting to the complaint Mr FISCHLER said that the matter will be investigated and if necessary legal proceedings will be instigated. The complaint received yesterday is quite similar to that received in early 1995, relating to the same border posts. As a result of this complaint the Commission veterinary services carried out an inspection and confirmed the veracity of many elements of the complaint. Subsequently during discussions the Italian authorities undertook to improve enforcement of the EU legislation on animal transport. Given that it is the responsibility of national authorities to ensure that EU legislation is enforced, if a further Commission inspection confirms that little has changed during the last 18 months as far as the treatment of animals imported through these border crossings is concerned, then the Commission could open infringement proceedings against the Italian Government.

COMMISSION SENDS REASONED OPINION TO GREECE FOR NON-IMPLEMENTATION OF ADIRECTIVE ON SHIPMENTS OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE. The European Commission has decided to send Greece a reasoned opinion concerning non-communication of national measures for the implementation by January 1994 of Council Directive 92/3/Euratom on transfrontier shipments of radioactive waste. This is one of the directives under the Euratom Treaty which aims at protecting workers and the population in general from ionizing radiation. It lays down procedures to control the transport of radioactive waste between Member States and its importation into and exportation from the Community. The deadline given to the Member State to incorporate this Directive into national law elapsed in January 1994. Greece has prepared draft legislation aimed at implementing this Directive, on which the Commission issued its recommendations in 1995, as foreseen by Article 33 of the Euratom Treaty. The Commission has not, however, received any further communications from Greece on this particular piece of legislation. Therefore the Commission, on the initiative of Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard, takes this further step to urge Greece to implement the Directive in order to avoid being taken to the Court of Justice.

COMMISSION ADOPTS A PROPOSAL ON THE BAN OF BEEF AND SHEEP TISSUES. The European Commission today adopted a proposal on the exclusion from the human food and animal feed chains of tissues which are most likely to be infective in the case of animals carrying the scrapie or BSE diseases. These tissues are the head, including the brain and eyes but excluding the tongue, and the spinal cord of cattle, of sheep and goats over 12 months of age and the spleen of sheep and goats irrespective the age. The proposal also prohibits the use of the vertebral column of cattle, sheep and goats for the production of mechanically recovered meat. The proposal will now be put forward to the Council of Agriculture Ministers for a decision [1] . Commenting on the proposal, Mr FISCHLER, Commissioner for Agriculture and Rural Development, said that the protection of human health and the restoration of consumer confidence in beef and sheep meat must be a top priority of the EU and that, in this context, all decisions relating to BSE should be firmly based on up to date and accurate scientific advice. The Commission's proposals are soundly based on the opinions of the Scientific Veterinary Committee and the World Health Organisation. It is regrettable therefore, he concluded, that the Standing Veterinary Committee voted against the proposed ban. BSE is thought to have arisen from sheep scrapie, although this is not confirmed. Recent experiments have shown that sheep can be infected by BSE, producing a disease clinically indistinguishable from scrapie. It is therefore possible that BSE is, in fact, a strain of scrapie. Furthermore, sheep in the Community have been fed on meat-and-bone meal, raising the possibility that some may have been infected with BSE On the basis of the advice of the World Health Organisation (3 April 1996) and the Scientific Veterinary Committee ( 21 October 1996) the Commission made this proposal with the view to eliminating from human food and animal feed those tissues most likely to be infective. While accepting that the risk is minimal, there is nevertheless a responsibility on the decision making bodies to take all action necessary to minimise this risk. As no Member State or third country can at present demonstrate freedom from all Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE's), it is proposed to prohibit the use of the specified risk materials from all countries. The possibility of a future derogation for third countries is foreseen. No such derogation is proposed for Member States, as scrapie probably occurs in all Member States. [1] Note : This decision can be taken by Council by a qualified majority or rejected by a simple majority of Member States within 15 days of the proposal being transmitted to Council. In the absence of one or other of the above conditions the Commission can take the decision.

the national measures they should have taken to transpose this legislation. 96/2040 - Belgium / 96/2047 -Portugal: Commission decides to send reasoned opinions to Belgium and Portugal for non-communication of measures implementing the Council Regulation on reduction of ports and pilotage dues for segregated ballast tanks. The European Commission has decided to send Belgium and Portugal reasoned opinions concerning non-communication of national measures for the implementation of Council Regulation 2978/94/EEC This Regulation aims at granting port and pilotage fees reduction to oil tankers which meet high environmental standards in order to encourage their use in EU waters. It should have been implemented by 31 December 1995. The purpose of this Regulation is twofold: the protection of the marine environment from pollution by oil tankers of a conventional design, and to avoid distortion of competition within the Union.

BSE: the Commission introduces a legal ban on the placing on the market of unsafe cosmetic products. In the framework of managing the problems linked to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and its possible consequences for human health, the European Commission has adopted a directive designed to ban the placing on the market of cosmetic products containing tissues and ingredients derived from the encephalon, spinal cord and eyes of bovine, ovine and caprine animals. This ban translates into legal terms a situation that already exists in the cosmetics industry. Indeed, this industry has for several years been implemented the recommendations of governmental and international agencies concerning BSE not to use bovine tissues or extracts of bovine tissues derived from the encephalon, the spinal cord and the eyes. This ban, which concerns the organs believed to present the greatest risks, is based on the precautionary principle. It is appropriate to take measures designed to ensure the safety and health of consumers without awaiting irrefutable proof of the link between BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease in humans. This ban is provisional and will be reviewed in line with the development of scientific knowledge. The Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive no later than 30 June 1997.

Service providers A French Decree of 25 November 1996 (96 1011) stipulates that ski instructors from other Member States can offer their services in France on condition that they notify their presence to the authorities. However, the French authorities can impose an aptitude test when there is a substantial difference between the candidates' technical competence and the relevant French standards. The Commission is verifying the conditions in which this Decree is applied. If it found that tests were imposed in cases where candidates have a qualification of another Member State which was equivalent to the French standards or that the aptitude tests were disproportionate, the Commission would not hesitate to open an infringement procedure against France.

The Commission wants to reinforce safety on aircraft operated by non-EU companies. Aircraft belonging to companies from non-EU countries that are suspected of non-compliance with international safety standards should be much more closely checked in the European Union, according to the European Commission which has just submitted a draft directive on this to the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament. The legislation proposed by Neil Kinnock, Commissioner responsible for Transport, provides for a detailed information exchange system on these aircraft between the Member States and the Commission. When non-compliance with international safety standards obviously threatens safety, the competent authority performing the inspection would be obliged to ground the plane. The directive would also allow the Commission to implement systematic surveillance measures and to restrict the operation of a specific operator or operators of a specific non-EU country. This proposal, drafted in the wake of the aircraft accident of Puerto Plata (in the Dominican Republic) in February 1996, which killed 176 European passengers, aims at ensuring an equivalent level of safety for all aircraft taking off from Community airports. In June 1996, a few months after the crash, the Commission issued a Communication "Defining a Community Aviation Safety Improvement Strategy". This described the steps necessary for a consistent and comprehensive strategy to improve aviation safety. Experience has shown that some non-EU countries do not always implement and enforce international safety standards. The Commission considers therefore that Member States should monitor non-EU countries aircraft in Community airports when there is suspicion that they do not comply with international safety standards. Common surveillance rules In order to ensure efficient monitoring, homogeneous, effective and well co-ordinated action is necessary. Therefore, the draft proposal includes a procedure for the safety assessment of foreign aircraft, in particular : - the collection and exchange of information. Collected data would come from various sources : passenger complaints, pilot and maintenance organisation reports, as well as information on any action taken subsequent to a ramp inspection or any follow-up information concerning the operator. - the ramp inspection. It would take place as soon as there is suspicion of non-compliance with international safety standards. The ramp inspection reports would be made available to the competent authorities of the Member States and the Commission, at their request. - the grounding of aircraft, when the deficiencies in compliance are clearly hazardous to safety, until the aircraft has been brought up to standard. The other Member States and the Commission, as well as the State responsible for the operation of the aircraft concerned, would be immediately informed. Systematic inspection Depending on the significance of the hazard to safety, and on the basis of the transmitted information, the Commission, with the assistance of an advisory committee composed of representatives of Member States, could decide : - systematic ramp inspection and other surveillance measures of a specific operator or of operators of a specific non-EU country - to ban or impose conditions on the operation of specific operators or operators of a specific non-EU country from Community airports, pending the adoption by the competent authority of

Commission takes further legal action against the United Kingdom for failing to respect EU rules on the protection of groundwater. The European Commission decided to send a Reasoned Opinion to the United Kingdom under Article 169 of the EC Treaty for its failure to fully comply with a Community directive for the protection of groundwater (Council Directive 80/68/EEC on the protection of groundwater against pollution caused by certain dangerous substances). This decision reflects the Commission's general concern that the vital Community's groundwater resources should be fully protected in accordance with the Directive. The Directive has the aims of preventing the introduction into groundwater of certain toxic, persistent and bioaccumulable substances and of limiting the introduction of certain other less hazardous substances into groundwater. With these aims in view, the Directive provides for a set of strict controls on activities which may lead to groundwater pollution, including in some cases prior authorisation and investigation. The decisions taken is a response to the following failures. The United Kingdom's transposal of the Directive in England and Wales and Northern Ireland is inadequate, in particular because prior authorisation and investigation of disposal is not required in all the situations provided for in the Directive. In addition, there is an inadequate application of the requirements of the Directive in relation to sheep dip disposal.

Food safety: first meeting of the renewed Multidisciplinary Scientific Committee(Brussels, 3 April 1997). Food safety: first meeting of the renewed Multidisciplinary Scientific Committee (Brussels, 3 April 1997) The Multidisciplinary Committee of the European Commission met today in Brussels for the first time in the new structure recently agreed by the Commission. The most important items on the agenda were: - the role and mandate of a new Scientific Committee for the risk evaluation of genetically modified organisms. - the review of the conditions for inactivation of the BSE agents during the industrial production of gelatine. On the first issue, the Committee agreed on the necessity to establish a specific Scientific Committee to advise the Commission on the use and commercialisation of genetically modified organisms and of products containing genetically modified organisms. On the other issue, the Committee definitively stressed that the technical treatment conditions set out in Commission Decision 96/362/EC of 11 June 1996 do not adequately guarantee the inactivation of the BSE agent. In such circumstances the Committee underlined that only non-infected primary bovine material can ensure a totally safe gelatine. It should be pointed out that the Commission's decision of 11 June set out a number of pre-conditions which when met would allow the Commission to consider the lifting of the export ban on UK bovine derived gelatine. To date the UK authorities have not informed the Commission that these pre-conditions have been fulfilled. Furthermore in the light of information which became available to the Commission after the 11 June decision which cast some doubt on the scientific basis of that decision, Mr FISCHLER has on a number of occasions emphasised that no approval for the export of UK bovine derived gelatine would be granted by the Commission until such time as the Commission was satisfied on the basis of scientific evidence, as to the treatment and processing procedures necessary to ensure the products safety. Ms Emma BONINO, Commissioner responsible for Consumer Policy and Consumer Health Protection, declared today that "I shall draw the attention of the Commission to the necessity of taking into account this advice of the Scientific Committee in reexamining its decision of 11 June 1996 concerning the partial and conditional lifting of the ban on gelatine exports derived from British bovine products". Moreover, Commissioner Bonino regretted that partial and not entirely correct informations were released in advance by Commission sources.

Commission opens infringement proceedings against 10 member states in relation to BSE. Commission opens infringement proceedings against 10 member states in relation to BSE The European Commission on 26 June 1997 decided to open the first stage of infringement proceedings under Article 169 of the EC Treaty against 10 Member States in respect of their apparent partial failure to implement and/or enforce some aspects of European Union (EU) Legislation concerning Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathies (BSE). The Member States are : France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Germany , Spain, Sweden, Finland, Italy and Portugal. The decision concerns the first stage of the proceedings, namely the dispatch of letters of formal notice giving the Member States concerned the opportunity of submitting their observations within one month. The presumed infringements are principally inadequate implementation of Commission Decision 96/449/EC (heat treatment system for processing animal waste) and failure to sufficiently control the respect of Commission Decision 94/381/EC prohibiting the use of mammalian tissues in feeding stuffs destined for ruminants. Commenting on the decision, Mr Franz FISCHLER, Commissioner for Agriculture and Rural Development, said that the meticulous implementation of all legislation relating to BSE is vital if it is to be eradicated and the possible risks to human health pending eradication are to be avoided. Given that some of the shortfalls could be relatively easily resolved, Mr FISCHLER expressed the hope that member states would address these matters as soon as possible so that the infringement procedures can be terminated. 1. France which has failed to implement Decision 96/449/EC on the grounds that it disputes the efficacy of the technical parameters for processing animal waste imposed by the decision and questions the legal basis on which the text was adopted. 2. Belgium and 3. Luxembourg inadequate measures adopted to enforce respect Decision 94/381/EC 4. Netherlands Failure to complete approval of all plants processing animal waste and failure to provide list of all plants concerned. Also incomplete implementation of Decision 96/449/EC 5. Germany Failure to implement Decision 96/449/EC as far as particle size parameter is concerned. Also national exemption from the requirements of processing under Decision 96/449/EC of certain by-products used for animal feed of processing material fit for human consumption. 6. Spain - Spain maintains that low risk material processed into animal feed need not be treated in accordance with the parameters of Directive 96/449/EC, - inadequate enforcement of feed ban imposed by Decision 94/381/EC because no official analysis of feed to detect mammalian meat and bone meal is made, - failure to ensure that a waste processing plant had had its processing procedures validated as required by Community Legislation. 7. Sweden - Failure to transpose Article 3 (2) of Directive 90/667/EC by the due date, - Failure to officially approve rendering plants as required by Article 4(1) of Directive 90/667/EEC, - Commission's interpretation of Decision 96/449/EC as far as processing of bones fit for human consumption into animal feed is disputed by Sweden, - Sweden's enforcement of the ban under Decision 94/381/EC of incorporating mammalian material in ruminant feed is considered inadequate in so far as the Swedish

control régime only envisages annual analysis of 100 samples. 8. Finland Inadequate enforcement of feed ban under Decision 94/381/EC as inadequate controls imposed to detect mammalian protein in ruminant feed (notably no microscopic tests). 9. Italy Control of the respect of the ban on feeding mammalian material to ruminants (Decision 94/381/EC) is inadequate. 10. Portugal Failure to co-operate with Commission in answering its written requests for information - breach of Article 5 of the EC Treaty. In respect of the United Kingdom the number of veterinary inspection visits which have taken place, the obligation imposed on that Member State to supply reports on BSE developments every 2 weeks and the meticulous attention of the Commission to the examination of National Legislation, complaints, press reports etc. appears at the present time to have prevented the maintenance of prima facie infringements. The Commission Veterinary Inspectorate envisage a series of missions during the current year in order to update information on compliance with their Community obligations in respect of BSE of all Member States including those not subject to the infringement proceedings now being opened. The Commission is also currently examining a number of complaints against Member States where it is alleged that single market obligations have been infringed by unilateral national measures going beyond those introduced at the Community level.
